hook: The boy genius of Bukhara whose medical book was used for 600 years.

pages.x: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born in 980 near Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan. By ten he knew the Quran by heart. At 16 he took up medicine, which he called "not one of the difficult sciences", and by 18 he was treating patients.

At 17 he cured the ruler of Bukhara of an illness his court doctors could not treat. As a reward he asked only to use the royal library, full of rare books, where he said he learned everything he knew. Soon afterwards the library burned down.

He read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times and still could not understand it, until a bookseller in the market talked him into buying a little book by al-Farabi for three coins. Suddenly it all made sense. He was so happy he gave money to the poor.

When his patrons fell, he wandered across Persia, serving rulers as doctor and minister. He was jailed, escaped disguised as a Sufi, and wrote at night, drinking wine to stay awake. He wrote some 450 works, of which about 240 survive.
His Canon of Medicine gathered Greek and Islamic medicine into five books, on diseases, drugs, infection and quarantine, and how to test a new medicine.
pages.fx: Translated into Latin, it was a main medical textbook in Europe for 600 years, and was still taught in some universities in the 1600s.

pages.x: He imagined a man created floating in the air, blindfolded, touching nothing at all. Would he know that he existed? Yes, said Avicenna, so the mind knows itself apart from the body. Six centuries later Descartes made a similar argument famous.

Avicenna was the most famous doctor and philosopher of the Islamic golden age. His Canon shaped medicine in the Muslim world and Europe for centuries, and his philosophy influenced Muslim and Christian thinkers alike.
pages.cap: His tomb at Hamadan in Iran
pts: Wrote the Canon of Medicine, used for 600 years
A leading philosopher of the Islamic world
Wrote around 450 works on almost every science
